items.title: What an audit report is actually for
items.summary: A fund that collects thousands of crores and spends lakhs is not a scandal by arithmetic alone. It is a question about intent.

body.text: The number is not the story

Every few months a figure surfaces that looks damning on its own: money in, very little money out. The gap gets a headline, the headline gets a hashtag, and the argument ends there. But a balance is not a verdict. Funds are allowed to hold money. Endowments are supposed to. The question an audit exists to answer is narrower and harder: was the money held for a stated purpose, and does the holding match that purpose?
What to look for instead

Read the audit for three things. First, the mandate — what the fund said it would do with the money when it asked for it. Second, the disbursement schedule, which tells you whether slow spending was planned or simply happened. Third, the auditor's own language: statutory auditors are careful people, and a qualified opinion is a much louder signal than a large unspent balance.
Why this matters beyond one fund

Public money attracts two failures at once — the failure to spend it well, and the failure to scrutinise it well. A press cycle that treats every unspent rupee as theft trains readers to ignore the cases that are theft. Precision is not pedantry here. It is the only thing that makes the accusation mean anything when it is finally warranted.

items.title: Support Global Voices’ January Spotlight: Independent journalism
items.summary: In our January spotlight, Global Voices is celebrating the independent journalism that keeps governments and institutions accountable.

body.text: Donate to our Independent Journalism Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!
Originally published on Global Voices
Image made via Canva Pro. All images fair use.

Journalism has been a vital part of society for centuries. Writing about what happened and sharing it with others; reading about what happened somewhere else and discussing it with those around you; having a platform for letters, comments, and opinion about everything from the niche to the rich. Journalism has toppled governments and CEOs, revealed complicated scams, brought out the beauty of ethnographically observed daily life, recorded our qualms and foibles for posterity, and whipped up outrage, empathy, and triumph.

But journalism is on a precipice. The shift from print to digital has opened up new possibilities, as well as vulnerabilities. Changes in how we interact, especially at a distance, have changed what (and how) people want to read, listen to, or watch to understand the news.

This decade has seen dramatic changes in the field, from the loss of foundational trust in the institution, to digital, legal, and physical threats to journalists to the near-complete erosion of financial security for people who carry out this work. Increasingly authoritarian governments turn on the media, and the press in countries from Hong Kong to Myanmar to Russia to Nicaragua has been forced into exile.

Even countries such as the UK and the US have seen government targeting of journalists for critical reporting. Israel’s genocide in Gaza has laid bare the hypocrisy of the international press establishment, causing a crisis of confidence, while small local news outlets and independent journalists continue to report despite this.

Through it all, journalists have kept documenting, analyzing, responding, and reporting, even when they are underpaid and overworked, face hostile governments and terrible technology, sometimes from exile, in terrible conditions, even at risk of their lives. As we begin 2027, Global Voices will turn the spotlight onto these voices that continue to speak truth to power and bring to light the news that we all need to know. We will look at civic journalism, find out what is changing, and meet some of these indefatigable defenders of our right to free speech and our right to information.

items.title: Net migration to UK at lowest level since 1997
items.summary: Net migration to Britain has fallen to the lowest level this century, excluding the Covid pandemic. Official data shows the number was 77,000 in the year ending in June - down about 90% from a peak in 2023. Tougher rules introduced in response to public concern have made it harder for people to come to work or study in the UK. Asylum claims are also down. Also: Israel has carried out more deadly airstrikes in the Gaza Strip, despite the ceasefire. A court in Kenya rules that the government breached the constitution by permitting the construction of an Ebola quarantine facility at a military base. US and South Korean researchers have created tiny robots which they hope could be used to treat patients with brain tumours. The BBC hears desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran. The Egyptian authorities say they have arrested a man on suspicion of causing a huge fire that killed 31 people when a fuel tanker overturned on a busy road in Cairo. The Norwegian low-cost airline, Norse Atlantic Airways, cancels all its flights, saying it faces a critical financial situation. And the British actress Helen Mirren launches a campaign to protect ancient olive groves in Italy which are threatened by an insect-borne bacterium. The Global News Podcast brings you the breaking news you need to hear, as it happens. Listen for the latest headlines and current affairs from around the world.…

items.title: Immune cells
items.summary: Every day, billions of specialised cells work to protect your body from harm. From the common cold and infections to cuts and scrapes or cancerous cells, our bodies deal with a range of potential threats and risks as we move through the world. The immune system is a complex and carefully orchestrated network connecting organs, tissues, and billions of specialised cells. Those cells have a variety of different roles as they respond to pathogens or harm, including engulfing microbes, identifying damage, or producing antibodies. Misha Glenny and his guests examine the different types of cells involved in an immune response, how they know what to respond to, and what happens when those cells aren’t working as they should. This In Our Time episode discusses why our immune cells are vital to life – both for us as individuals, and as a species. The discussion explores the interconnected nature of the immune system, and what we know actually affects the way our immune cells function. With Sheena Cruickshank Professor of Immunology at the University of Manchester Dan Davis Author and Professor of Immunology at Imperial College London And Emily Gwyer Findlay Professor of Inflammation Biology at the University of Southampton Producer: Martha Owen Reading list: Daniel M Davis, ‘Immune Health: A Myth-Busting Guide’ (Vintage, 2026) John Tregoning, ‘Infectious’ (Oneworld, 2021) In Our Time…
